Chapter overview

Dravidian Movement traces the transition from linguistic and anti-caste foundations through non-Brahmin organisation, Justice and Self-Respect convergence, Dravidar Kazhagam, DMK, language agitations, electoral power and the later DMK–AIADMK party system.

FoundationsJustice, Self-Respect & DKDMK organisation & cultureAgitations & electionsGovernment & party system
Scope, Meaning and Major Historical Phases

The Dravidian Movement developed through linguistic research, anti-caste reform, non-Brahmin politics, Self-Respect activism, Dravidar Kazhagam and later electoral parties rather than emerging from one event.

Meaning of the Dravidian Movement

The Dravidian Movement was a broad social, cultural and political movement that developed in the Madras Presidency and later became centred principally in Tamil Nadu.

It addressed issues such as:

  • Caste hierarchy
  • Social representation
  • Education
  • Public employment
  • Rationalism
  • Women’s rights
  • Language
  • Regional identity
  • Centre–State relations
  • Political power

It was not created by one leader or organisation at one moment.

It developed through several overlapping stages.

Major Historical Phases
Intellectual and Cultural Foundations

Important nineteenth-century developments included:

  • Recognition of the Dravidian language family
  • Recovery of classical Tamil literature
  • Anti-caste thought
  • Tamil print expansion
  • Growth of Tamil cultural consciousness
Non-Brahmin Political Phase

Important organisations included:

  • Madras Non-Brahmin Association
  • Madras United League
  • Madras Dravidian Association
  • South Indian Liberal Federation or Justice Party
Self-Respect Phase

From 1925, the Self-Respect Movement introduced a more radical programme involving:

  • Caste abolition
  • Rationalism
  • Women’s emancipation
  • Marriage reform
  • Opposition to hereditary religious authority
Dravidar Kazhagam Phase

In 1944, the Justice Party was transformed into Dravidar Kazhagam under Periyar.

Electoral Dravidian Phase

In 1949, Anna and his associates founded the DMK.

The DMK:

  • Entered elections
  • Built mass organisations
  • Used public culture and cinema
  • Became the principal opposition
  • Formed the state government in 1967
Two-Party Dravidian Phase

After the formation of AIADMK in 1972, the DMK and AIADMK became the two principal Dravidian political parties of Tamil Nadu.

Linguistic, Cultural and Anti-Caste Foundations

Its foundations combined the Dravidian language-family idea, Tamil classical recovery and distinct anti-caste strategies developed by thinkers and community organisers.

Dravidian Language Family

The word “Dravidian” first gained major modern importance through linguistic study.

Important scholars included:

  • F. W. Ellis
  • Robert Caldwell

In 1816, Ellis argued that the South Indian languages belonged to a family separate from Indo-Aryan languages.

In 1856, Caldwell published:

  • A Comparative Grammar of the Dravidian or South-Indian Family of Languages

The study compared languages including:

  • Tamil
  • Telugu
  • Kannada
  • Malayalam

This linguistic classification later acquired cultural and political meanings.

Tamil Renaissance

The recovery of classical texts by scholars such as:

  • C. W. Damodaram Pillai
  • U. V. Swaminatha Iyer
  • Arumuga Navalar
  • Other Tamil editors

created greater awareness of:

  • Sangam literature
  • Ancient Tamil society
  • Tamil grammatical tradition
  • Tamil rulers and ports
  • Jain and Buddhist literary contributions
Anti-Caste Intellectual Foundations

Important earlier anti-caste thinkers included:

  • Ayya Vaikundar
  • Vallalar
  • Iyothee Thass
  • Rettamalai Srinivasan
  • M. C. Rajah

Their approaches differed.

Iyothee Thass

He promoted:

  • Casteless Dravidian identity
  • Buddhism
  • Education
  • Historical reinterpretation
  • Rejection of Hindu caste identity
Rettamalai Srinivasan

He promoted:

  • Community organisation
  • Journalism
  • Political representation
  • Civil rights
From Language to Political Identity

“Dravidian” gradually came to indicate more than a language family.

It was used to express:

  • A South Indian cultural identity
  • Opposition to Sanskrit-centred superiority
  • Non-Brahmin political unity
  • Tamil historical dignity
  • Opposition to North Indian cultural domination

The linguistic meaning and political meaning of “Dravidian” must not be treated as identical.

From Non-Brahmin Movement to Dravidian Political Identity

Early non-Brahmin associations converted unequal educational and administrative access into organised representation demands and gradually adopted a positive Dravidian political identity.

Early Non-Brahmin Organisations

Educated non-Brahmin leaders believed that access to:

  • Higher education
  • Government employment
  • Professional occupations
  • Legislative institutions

was distributed unequally.

Important organisations included:

  • Madras Non-Brahmin Association — 1909
  • Madras United League — 1912
  • Madras Dravidian Association
  • Dravidian Home
Dravidian Home

Dr. C. Natesa Mudaliar established the Dravidian Home at Triplicane.

It provided:

  • Accommodation for non-Brahmin students
  • Educational assistance
  • Social networks
  • Political awareness
South Indian Liberal Federation

The South Indian Liberal Federation was founded in 1916.

It became popularly known as the:

  • Justice Party

Its principal founders were:

  • P. Theagaraya Chetty
  • T. M. Nair
  • C. Natesa Mudaliar
Non-Brahmin Manifesto

The manifesto of 1916 demanded:

  • Public-service representation
  • Educational opportunity
  • Legislative safeguards
  • Protection from social monopoly
Identity Transformation

Initially, “non-Brahmin” was mainly a political category describing different communities outside Brahmin groups.

The term “Dravidian” supplied a more positive historical and cultural identity.

It suggested:

  • Shared South Indian ancestry
  • A common linguistic background
  • Resistance to Aryan or Sanskritic domination
  • A wider political community

However, the different non-Brahmin communities did not possess identical social interests. Intermediate castes, Adi Dravidas, Muslims, Christians, landholders and workers often had distinct demands.

Justice Party, Self-Respect Movement and Organisational Convergence

Justice Party constitutional politics and Self-Respect social reform remained distinct at first but converged during the 1930s under common anti-caste and anti-Hindi campaigns.

Justice Party Contribution

The Justice Party introduced:

  • Electoral non-Brahmin politics
  • Communal representation
  • Expanded educational access
  • Women’s qualified franchise
  • Adi Dravida welfare measures
  • Regulation of religious endowments

Its main method was:

  • Constitutional politics
  • Legislative councils
  • Elections
  • Government Orders
Self-Respect Movement

The Self-Respect Movement began in 1925 under Periyar.

It addressed:

  • Caste abolition
  • Untouchability
  • Rationalism
  • Priestly authority
  • Marriage reform
  • Women’s equality
  • Religious criticism

Its main methods included:

  • Public conferences
  • Propaganda tours
  • Newspapers
  • Reform marriages
  • Inter-dining
  • Social campaigns
Organisational Difference
Justice Party
  • Political party
  • Contested elections
  • Formed governments
  • Worked within the colonial constitution
Self-Respect Movement
  • Social-reform movement
  • Did not initially seek electoral office
  • Sought transformation of daily social practices
Growing Cooperation

During the 1930s:

  • Justice Party leaders attended Self-Respect conferences.
  • Self-Respect activists defended communal representation.
  • Both opposed Congress domination.
  • Both participated in the first Anti-Hindi agitation.
  • Periyar’s social programme increasingly influenced the Justice Party.
Periyar’s Leadership

Following the Justice Party’s defeat in the 1937 election, Periyar became its president in 1938.

This brought the party’s political organisation and the Self-Respect Movement’s social programme closer together.

The convergence prepared the way for the formation of Dravidar Kazhagam in 1944.

Salem Conference and the Formation of Dravidar Kazhagam

The Salem Conference of 1944 transformed the electoral Justice Party into the non-electoral Dravidar Kazhagam shaped by rationalist and Self-Respect principles.

Salem Conference

The major Justice Party conference was held at:

  • Salem
  • 27 August 1944

At the conference, the Justice Party was transformed into:

  • Dravidar Kazhagam
  • Common abbreviation — DK

The resolutions are often associated with:

  • Periyar
  • C. N. Annadurai
  • Other Justice Party and Self-Respect leaders
Major Organisational Changes

Members were encouraged or required to:

  • Renounce British titles
  • Give up nominated public offices
  • Remove caste suffixes
  • Withdraw from electoral competition
  • Concentrate on social transformation
  • Promote Dravidian identity
  • Adopt rationalist and Self-Respect ideas
Why the Name Changed

The name “Justice Party” was associated with:

  • Colonial-era elections
  • Elite leadership
  • Provincial ministries
  • Cooperation with British authority

The name Dravidar Kazhagam represented:

  • A broader social movement
  • Dravidian identity
  • Anti-caste transformation
  • Rationalism
  • Non-electoral social action
Meaning of Kazhagam

“Kazhagam” can mean:

  • Association
  • Federation
  • Organisation

Dravidar Kazhagam may therefore be translated broadly as:

  • Dravidian Federation
  • Dravidian Association
Historical Importance

The transformation marked the end of the Justice Party as an ordinary electoral organisation.

Dravidar Kazhagam became:

  • A social movement
  • A propaganda organisation
  • A rationalist body
  • An anti-caste organisation
  • An ideological foundation for later Dravidian parties

Periyar founded the Self-Respect Movement but did not originally found the Justice Party. He later transformed the Justice Party into DK.

Dravidar Kazhagam, Black Shirts and Social Propaganda

DK used black-shirt volunteers, publications, symbolic protest and social propaganda instead of elections to challenge caste, religion, language domination and gender inequality.

Non-Electoral Organisation

Dravidar Kazhagam rejected electoral office as its primary method.

It argued that electoral politics could:

  • Encourage personal ambition
  • Weaken social reform
  • Produce compromise
  • Place party success above ideological change

DK therefore concentrated on:

  • Conferences
  • Demonstrations
  • Publications
  • Social reform
  • Rationalist propaganda
  • Anti-caste campaigns
Black Shirt Volunteers

The Black Shirt Volunteer Corps developed during 1945–1946.

The black shirt symbolised:

  • Protest
  • Social humiliation experienced under caste
  • Opposition to superstition
  • Determination to fight inequality

A major Black Shirt conference was held in:

  • Madurai
  • May 1946

The conference venue faced violent opposition and was attacked.

DK Flag

The DK flag used:

  • Black background
  • Red circle at the centre

The colours broadly represented:

Black
  • Oppression
  • Degradation
  • Protest
Red
  • Social transformation
  • Revolution
  • Human liberation
Major Campaigns

DK propaganda addressed:

  • Caste titles
  • Religious authority
  • Untouchability
  • Hindi imposition
  • Women’s inequality
  • Superstition
  • Social representation
Methods

Methods included:

  • Black-flag demonstrations
  • Street meetings
  • Public debates
  • Processions
  • Pamphlets
  • Symbolic protests
  • Social-reform marriages
  • Rationalist publications
Publications

Important publications included:

  • Kudi Arasu
  • Viduthalai
  • Dravida Nadu
  • Other movement journals

The Dravida Nadu journal was associated principally with Anna and later the DMK current.

The complete rationalist publication sequence belongs to Chapter 23.

Periyar, Anna and the Emerging Organisational Differences

Periyar and Anna shared major social objectives but differed over elections, independence, organisation, generational strategy and democratic political participation.

Periyar and Anna

C. N. Annadurai joined the Justice–Self-Respect political current during the 1930s.

He became known as:

  • Anna
  • Perarignar Anna

He contributed through:

  • Public speaking
  • Journalism
  • Theatre
  • Political essays
  • Organisation

Periyar and Anna agreed on many issues, including:

  • Opposition to caste hierarchy
  • Communal representation
  • Rationalism
  • Tamil and Dravidian identity
  • Opposition to compulsory Hindi
  • Social reform
Major Differences
Electoral Politics

Periyar

  • Distrusted elections
  • Preferred non-electoral social transformation

Anna

  • Believed elections could be used to implement social reform
  • Wanted the movement to enter democratic institutions
Indian Independence

Periyar regarded 15 August 1947 as insufficient social liberation and criticised the transfer of power without caste abolition.

Anna regarded the end of British rule as an important achievement, even while maintaining criticism of social inequality.

Organisational Strategy

Periyar preferred:

  • Central ideological discipline
  • Social propaganda
  • Movement independence from elections

Anna preferred:

  • Mass party organisation
  • Electoral participation
  • Youth mobilisation
  • Wider public communication
Marriage to Maniammai

Periyar’s marriage to Maniammai in 1949 intensified the organisational dispute.

However, the division should not be explained by the marriage alone.

Differences over:

  • Elections
  • Democracy
  • Leadership succession
  • Generational strategy
  • Political participation

had already developed.

Historical Caution

The DMK split was both:

  • Personal
  • Organisational
  • Strategic
  • Generational

Reducing it to only one private event gives an incomplete explanation.

Formation of the Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam

Anna and his associates founded the DMK in 1949 as a mass political organisation prepared to use elections while retaining major Dravidian social themes.

Formation

The Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam was founded on:

  • 17 September 1949

The public founding meeting was held at:

  • Robinson Park
  • Royapuram
  • Madras

The organisation is commonly abbreviated as:

  • DMK

Its name may be translated as:

  • Dravidian Progressive Federation
Founding Leader

C. N. Annadurai became the party’s:

  • General Secretary
  • Principal organiser
  • Ideological and public leader

The post of party president was initially left vacant as a symbolic acknowledgement of Periyar’s earlier leadership.

Important Early Leaders

Early leaders included:

  • C. N. Annadurai
  • V. R. Nedunchezhiyan
  • E. V. K. Sampath
  • M. Karunanidhi
  • K. A. Mathiazhagan
  • N. V. Natarajan
  • K. Anbazhagan
  • Sathyavani Muthu
  • N. S. Krishnan and cultural supporters
  • Other district-level organisers
Meaning of Munnetram

“Munnetram” means:

  • Progress
  • Advancement
  • Development

The name suggested that the organisation sought to convert Dravidian social ideas into forward political action.

DK and DMK
Dravidar Kazhagam
  • Led by Periyar
  • Non-electoral
  • Concentrated on social transformation
Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam
  • Led by Anna
  • Prepared for electoral politics
  • Developed a mass party structure

The DMK was an organisational split from DK, but it retained major elements of the earlier movement’s social language.

Early DMK Leadership, Organisation and Publications

The early DMK developed local branches, publications, orators, youth networks and internal organisation that converted propaganda into disciplined party mobilisation.

Party Structure

The DMK built an organisation based on:

  • Local branches
  • Town branches
  • District bodies
  • General Council
  • Executive committees
  • Youth groups
  • Women’s groups
  • Cultural troupes
  • Publication networks

Tea shops, reading rooms, salons and local meeting points became centres of political discussion.

Murasoli

Murasoli began in:

  • 1942
  • Initially as a handwritten or cyclostyled publication

It was founded by:

  • M. Karunanidhi

It later became:

  • An important DMK publication
  • A regular newspaper
  • A vehicle for party communication
Dravida Nadu

The journal Dravida Nadu was associated with:

  • C. N. Annadurai
  • Dravidian political discussion
  • Social criticism
  • Regional autonomy
  • Language rights
Nam Naadu

Nam Naadu became an important DMK-associated publication during the party’s expansion.

Public Orators

The party developed a large group of speakers, including:

  • Anna
  • Nedunchezhiyan
  • E. V. K. Sampath
  • Karunanidhi
  • K. A. Mathiazhagan
  • Anbazhagan
  • Kannadasan
  • Other district speakers
Cadre Development

DMK branches encouraged:

  • Reading
  • Debate
  • Public speaking
  • Political writing
  • Organisational elections
  • Fundraising
  • Street propaganda

The party’s disciplined local network distinguished it from movements based only on prominent leaders.

Symbol and Flag

The DMK adopted:

  • Red and black colours
  • Rising Sun election symbol

The Rising Sun came to represent:

  • Emergence from darkness
  • Social awakening
  • Political change

Party history should distinguish the DK flag, which contains a red circle, from the DMK’s red-and-black party flag.

Women, Adi Dravidas, Workers and Grassroots Participation

Women, Adi Dravidas, workers, students and urban lower-income communities widened the movement while also exposing continuing inequalities inside broad Dravidian coalitions.

Women’s Participation

Women participated as:

  • Speakers
  • Organisers
  • Election workers
  • Writers
  • Protesters
  • Conference delegates
  • Local-branch members

Important women associated with the broader Dravidian movement included:

  • Nagammai
  • Maniammai
  • Moovalur Ramamirtham
  • S. Dharmambal
  • Sathyavani Muthu
  • Kunjitham Gurusamy
  • Other district activists
Maniammai

Maniammai became important within Dravidar Kazhagam through:

  • Organisational work
  • Publications
  • Management of movement institutions
  • Continuation of DK after Periyar’s death

Her detailed contribution belongs mainly to the Periyar and movement-legacy discussions.

Sathyavani Muthu

Sathyavani Muthu became an important:

  • Adi Dravida leader
  • DMK organiser
  • Legislator
  • Minister

Her career also reveals tensions concerning Dalit representation within broad Dravidian parties.

Adi Dravida Participation

The movement supported:

  • Reservation
  • Educational opportunity
  • Temple entry
  • Removal of untouchability
  • Social dignity

However, Dalit activists argued that broad non-Brahmin or Dravidian unity could conceal caste inequality between:

  • Intermediate communities
  • Communities subjected to untouchability
Workers and Urban Poor

DMK gained support among:

  • Textile workers
  • Transport workers
  • Small traders
  • Rickshaw workers
  • Urban lower-middle classes
  • Students
  • Slum residents
Grassroots Communication

The movement spread through:

  • Tea shops
  • Reading rooms
  • Political drama
  • Cinema halls
  • Party newspapers
  • Street-corner meetings
  • Local festivals
  • Fan associations
Balanced Assessment

The Dravidian Movement widened political participation, but it did not automatically eliminate:

  • Caste violence
  • Patriarchy
  • Unequal party leadership
  • Under-representation of Dalit women
  • Economic inequality

The distinction between ideological equality and actual social power must be maintained.

Theatre, Literature, Oratory and Tamil Cinema

Oratory, theatre, literature and cinema made complex political ideas accessible and created an unusually close relationship between popular culture and party organisation.

Public Oratory

The Dravidian Movement developed a distinctive style of public speaking.

Its speeches used:

  • Accessible Tamil
  • Humour
  • Historical references
  • Questions
  • Satire
  • Literary quotations
  • Emotional appeals
  • Social criticism

Public speaking enabled leaders to reach people with limited formal education.

Theatre

Political plays discussed:

  • Caste
  • Religion
  • Social inequality
  • Language
  • Labour
  • Women’s oppression
  • Political corruption

Important dramatists and writers included:

  • C. N. Annadurai
  • M. Karunanidhi
  • Bharathidasan
  • K. R. Ramasamy
  • M. R. Radha
  • Other movement artists
Anna’s Plays

Important works associated with Anna include:

  • Velaikkari
  • Or Iravu
  • Other social and political plays
Karunanidhi’s Writing

Karunanidhi wrote:

  • Plays
  • Screenplays
  • Film dialogues
  • Political essays
  • Historical fiction
  • Newspaper articles
Parasakthi

The film Parasakthi was released in:

  • 1952

Important associations:

  • Dialogue — M. Karunanidhi
  • Lead actor — Sivaji Ganesan
  • Social and religious criticism
  • Powerful courtroom and public speeches
Cinema as Political Communication

Films transmitted Dravidian ideas through:

  • Dialogues
  • Songs
  • Heroic characters
  • Criticism of hypocrisy
  • Tamil linguistic pride
  • Images of social injustice

The DMK used cinema more systematically than earlier Indian political organisations.

Actors and Politics

Important film personalities associated with the movement included:

  • N. S. Krishnan
  • K. R. Ramasamy
  • Sivaji Ganesan
  • M. G. Ramachandran
  • S. S. Rajendran
  • M. R. Radha

Not all remained in the same organisation throughout their careers.

Historical Importance

The relationship between cinema and politics allowed:

  • Political messages to reach mass audiences
  • Actors to become political organisers
  • Fan clubs to become mobilisation networks
  • Party language to enter everyday conversation

Academic studies identify public oratory, theatre and cinema as central to the strength of Tamil subnational and Dravidian political mobilisation.

Early DMK Agitations: Kallakudi, Education and Tamil Identity

Kallakudi, opposition to the modified elementary-education scheme and Tamil-name campaigns connected regional dignity with education, caste occupation and economic power.

Three-Point Agitation of 1953

The DMK organised major agitations in 1953 around several issues.

These included:

  • Kallakudi name agitation
  • Opposition to Rajaji’s modified elementary-education scheme
  • Protest concerning national political criticism of the party
Kallakudi Agitation

A cement company connected with industrialist Ramkrishna Dalmia used the name:

  • Dalmiapuram

for the Kallakudi industrial area.

DMK activists demanded restoration of the Tamil place name:

  • Kallakudi

On:

  • 15 July 1953

protesters led by M. Karunanidhi:

  • Altered station nameboards
  • Organised a railway blockade
  • Lay on the railway track

Police action resulted in deaths and injuries.

Karunanidhi and other protesters were imprisoned.

Historical Meaning

Kallakudi was presented as a struggle against:

  • Erasure of Tamil place names
  • North Indian economic and cultural dominance
  • Disrespect for regional identity
Modified Scheme of Elementary Education

Rajaji’s government introduced a revised elementary-education scheme during 1953.

Opponents called it:

  • Hereditary Education Scheme
  • Kula Kalvi Thittam

Critics argued that children might be directed towards family occupations and that the scheme could reinforce:

  • Caste-based labour
  • Hereditary occupation
  • Rural inequality

The DMK and other opponents organised campaigns against it.

The scheme was withdrawn after K. Kamaraj became Chief Minister.

Tamil Name and State Identity

The movement also demanded:

  • Greater use of Tamil
  • Protection of Tamil place names
  • Recognition of Tamil Nadu as the state’s name
  • Opposition to perceived cultural domination

These campaigns connected daily administrative questions with larger regional identity.

Electoral Entry and the 1957 Election

The 1957 election was the DMK’s first major electoral test and established a legislative presence through fifteen Assembly victories.

Debate over Elections

The DMK did not immediately enter elections after its formation.

Some members feared electoral participation would:

  • Weaken ideological discipline
  • Produce personal ambition
  • Encourage compromise

Others argued that the party could not implement social change without legislative power.

Tiruchirappalli Conference

At the DMK state conference held at Tiruchirappalli during the mid-1950s, cadres were consulted about electoral participation.

A large majority supported contesting elections.

Election of 1957

The DMK contested the Madras Legislative Assembly election of:

  • 1957

It fielded approximately:

  • 150 Assembly candidates

The party won:

  • 15 Assembly seats

Because the party had not yet secured full official recognition in the expected form, several candidates contested under available symbols or classifications.

Important Winners and Leaders

The election brought leaders such as:

  • C. N. Annadurai
  • M. Karunanidhi
  • K. Anbazhagan
  • Sathyavani Muthu
  • Other DMK representatives

into legislative politics.

Importance

Although 15 seats did not make the DMK the principal governing alternative immediately, the result established that:

  • Dravidian social ideology possessed electoral support.
  • The party had moved beyond urban propaganda.
  • Its local branches could conduct election campaigns.
  • Tamil cultural politics could be converted into votes.

The 1957 election was the DMK’s first major electoral test.

Growth in 1962 and Emergence as the Principal Opposition

The 1962 result of fifty seats made the DMK the principal opposition and demonstrated durable organisation despite splits and Anna’s own Assembly defeat.

Election of 1962

In the 1962 Madras Legislative Assembly election, the DMK contested approximately:

  • 142 Assembly seats

It won:

  • 50 seats

The increase from 15 to 50 seats demonstrated rapid organisational growth.

Anna’s Defeat and Parliamentary Entry

Anna lost his Assembly constituency in the 1962 election.

He later entered:

  • Rajya Sabha

His speeches in Parliament brought national attention to:

  • Dravidian identity
  • Language rights
  • Federalism
  • State autonomy
  • Regional equality
Principal Opposition

The DMK became the principal opposition force in the state legislature.

This gave it:

  • Greater public visibility
  • Legislative experience
  • Recognition as the main alternative to Congress
  • Stronger district organisation
Price-Rise Agitations

During the early 1960s, the DMK organised protests concerning:

  • Food scarcity
  • Inflation
  • Rising prices
  • Public distribution
  • Economic distress

Many leaders and cadres faced arrest.

E. V. K. Sampath Split

E. V. K. Sampath left the DMK in 1961 and established the:

  • Tamil National Party

The split reflected disagreements concerning:

  • Dravida Nadu
  • Party leadership
  • Cultural methods
  • Electoral strategy

The DMK nevertheless expanded in the 1962 election.

Significance

The 1962 result demonstrated that the party’s strength came from more than:

  • One leader
  • Cinema
  • Anti-Hindi sentiment

It possessed a durable local party network and a growing social coalition.

Dravida Nadu Demand and Shift towards State Autonomy

The movement shifted from the separatist Dravida Nadu demand to state autonomy, federalism and language rights within India after changing constitutional and regional conditions.

Meaning of Dravida Nadu

Dravida Nadu referred to a proposed separate political unit for the Dravidian-speaking regions of South India.

Different versions imagined the unit as including:

  • Tamil-speaking areas
  • Telugu-speaking areas
  • Kannada-speaking areas
  • Malayalam-speaking areas
Background of the Demand

The demand arose from fears concerning:

  • Hindi domination
  • North Indian political power
  • Unequal federal relations
  • Brahminical cultural authority
  • Centralised administration
  • Protection of South Indian languages
DK Position

Periyar promoted a separate Dravidian political unit as a way to secure:

  • Social transformation
  • Cultural autonomy
  • Freedom from North Indian domination
DMK Position

The early DMK retained the Dravida Nadu demand.

Anna defended the right of self-determination while participating in democratic politics.

Practical Difficulties

The demand faced several problems:

  • Telugu, Kannada and Malayalam regions developed their own linguistic state movements.
  • The States Reorganisation Act of 1956 created separate linguistic states.
  • Other South Indian states did not adopt the DMK’s separatist programme.
  • Indian constitutional law opposed secession.
  • The Sino-Indian War of 1962 strengthened national-security concerns.
Sixteenth Constitutional Amendment

The Constitution (Sixteenth Amendment) Act of 1963 strengthened requirements concerning:

  • Sovereignty
  • Integrity of India
  • Electoral oaths

The DMK formally abandoned the demand for a separate Dravida Nadu in 1963.

New Emphasis

The party shifted towards:

  • State autonomy
  • Federalism
  • Greater powers for states
  • Language rights
  • Opposition to excessive centralisation
  • Financial decentralisation
Essential Distinction
Dravida Nadu
  • Separate sovereign or politically independent unit
  • Early DK and DMK demand
State Autonomy
  • Greater powers for states within the Indian Union
  • Later major DMK position

Anna stated that although the separatist demand had been abandoned, the grievances that produced it remained relevant.

Anti-Hindi Agitation of 1965

The 1965 Anti-Hindi agitation combined student-led mobilisation, party organisation and spontaneous protest over official-language equality and employment opportunity.

Official-Language Background

The Constitution provided that Hindi would become the official language of the Union while English would continue for a transitional period.

As the year 1965 approached, many non-Hindi-speaking people feared that:

  • English would be removed
  • Hindi would gain exclusive official status
  • Non-Hindi speakers would face disadvantage in Union employment and examinations
DMK Position

The DMK opposed:

  • Compulsory Hindi
  • Hindi as the sole official language
  • Linguistic inequality
  • Employment disadvantage for non-Hindi speakers

It supported:

  • Continued use of English
  • Equality among Indian languages
  • Protection of Tamil
  • Federal language rights
Students

Students became the most visible participants in the 1965 agitation.

Forms of protest included:

  • Class boycotts
  • Processions
  • Black flags
  • Public meetings
  • Railway and road blockades
  • Burning of Hindi materials
  • Hunger strikes
Violence and Repression

The agitation became intense during January and February 1965.

There were:

  • Clashes
  • Police firing
  • Arrests
  • Destruction of property
  • Deaths
  • Self-immolations

The precise death total differs between sources and should not be stated without identifying the source.

Role of the DMK

The movement included both:

  • Organised party activity
  • Student-led spontaneous protest

It is inaccurate to treat every incident as centrally directed by the DMK.

Political Consequences

The agitation:

  • Weakened Congress support
  • Strengthened the DMK
  • Made language a decisive election issue
  • Produced assurances that English would continue
  • Reinforced Tamil regional identity
Historical Distinction
Anti-Hindi Agitation of 1937–1940
  • Opposed compulsory Hindi in provincial schools
  • Directed against Rajaji’s education policy
Anti-Hindi Agitation of 1965
  • Concerned Union official-language policy
  • Led strongly by students
  • Occurred immediately before the DMK’s electoral rise

Academic research describes the 1965 mobilisation as both intense and partly decentralised, with spontaneous participation beyond formal party direction.

Election of 1967 and the First DMK Government

The 1967 election ended Congress rule in the state and enabled the first DMK government to enact major language, marriage and Tamil identity measures.

Political Background

Factors contributing to the Congress defeat included:

  • Food shortage
  • Price rise
  • Anti-Hindi sentiment
  • Public dissatisfaction
  • Growth of DMK organisation
  • Popularity of cinema-based campaigners
  • Opposition-party alliance
  • Decline of Congress dominance
Opposition Alliance

Anna constructed an electoral alliance including parties such as:

  • Swatantra Party
  • Communist parties or left groups in selected arrangements
  • Muslim League
  • Other anti-Congress forces

The alliance allowed opposition parties to avoid dividing votes in many constituencies.

Election Result

In the 1967 Madras Legislative Assembly election:

  • The DMK won a clear majority.
  • It secured 138 Assembly seats.
  • C. N. Annadurai became Chief Minister.

This was the first time:

  • A Dravidian party formed the government
  • The Congress lost power in the state
  • A non-Congress regional party achieved such a major state-level victory

Official election records confirm the DMK’s constituency victories and its transformation into the governing party.

Major Early Measures

The Anna government is associated with:

  • Legal recognition of Self-Respect marriages
  • Adoption of the two-language policy
  • Resolution to rename Madras State as Tamil Nadu
  • Subsidised-rice commitment
  • Strengthening Tamil cultural recognition

Detailed responsibility and legislative chronology belong to Chapter 29.

Self-Respect Marriages

Tamil Nadu inserted Section 7-A into the Hindu Marriage Act to recognise:

  • Suyamariyathai marriages
  • Seerthiruththa marriages

The law recognised ceremonies based on:

  • Mutual declaration
  • Exchange of garlands or rings
  • Tying of the thali where chosen
  • Presence of relatives or friends
Two-Language Policy

Tamil Nadu adopted a policy based mainly on:

  • Tamil
  • English

It rejected compulsory Hindi as part of the state school formula.

Name Tamil Nadu

The Assembly adopted the proposal to rename:

  • Madras State
  • As Tamil Nadu

The central law was enacted in 1968.

The new name came into effect on:

  • 14 January 1969

The legal effective date should not be confused with the Assembly resolution passed earlier under Anna.

AIADMK and the Expansion of the Dravidian Party System

The creation of ADMK in 1972 and its later development as AIADMK produced a competitive Dravidian party system dominated by DMK and AIADMK.

After Anna

Anna died in:

  • February 1969

M. Karunanidhi succeeded him as:

  • Chief Minister
  • Principal DMK leader

The DMK continued to develop:

  • Tamil identity politics
  • State-autonomy demands
  • Welfare programmes
  • Cinema-based mobilisation
  • Electoral organisation
M. G. Ramachandran

M. G. Ramachandran was popularly known as:

  • MGR

He was:

  • A major Tamil film star
  • A prominent DMK campaigner
  • An important organiser of popular support

His film image emphasised:

  • Protection of the poor
  • Justice
  • Charity
  • Opposition to corruption
  • Defence of women and workers
Split of 1972

MGR was expelled from the DMK following disputes involving:

  • Party leadership
  • Financial accountability
  • Organisational control
  • Political rivalry

He founded a new party in October 1972:

  • Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam
  • ADMK

It later became:

  • All India Anna Dravida Munnetra Kazhagam
  • AIADMK
Electoral Rise

The AIADMK:

  • Used MGR’s film popularity
  • Converted fan clubs into political networks
  • Presented itself as the true inheritor of Anna’s legacy
  • Combined Dravidian identity with welfare-oriented populism

MGR became Chief Minister in:

  • 1977
Dravidian Party System

From the 1970s, Tamil Nadu politics became dominated mainly by:

  • DMK
  • AIADMK

The two parties competed while sharing several broad commitments:

  • Social justice
  • Reservation
  • Tamil identity
  • State welfare
  • Regional political power
  • Opposition to exclusive Hindi dominance

They differed in:

  • Leadership style
  • Party organisation
  • Alliances
  • Welfare priorities
  • Interpretation of Dravidian ideology
Wider Dravidian Organisations

Other parties and movements later emerged from splits or reinterpretations, including:

  • MDMK
  • DMDK
  • Smaller Dravidian and Tamil-oriented parties

Not every party using “Dravidian” in its name follows the same ideology or organisational lineage.

Historical Importance

The movement developed through three different organisational forms:

1. Justice Party — electoral non-Brahmin representation 2. Dravidar Kazhagam — non-electoral social revolution 3. DMK and AIADMK — mass electoral Dravidian politics

The DMK and AIADMK became rival dominant parties rather than one continuous organisation.

Rapid Revision and High-Yield Distinctions

The final topic consolidates chronology, organisations, leaders, publications, movements, elections and the distinctions most likely to appear in TNPSC examinations.

Essential Chronology
  • 1816 — Ellis argued for a separate South Indian language family
  • 1856 — Caldwell’s Comparative Grammar
  • 1909 — Madras Non-Brahmin Association
  • 1912 — Madras United League
  • 1916 — South Indian Liberal Federation formed
  • 1916 — Non-Brahmin Manifesto
  • 1925 — Self-Respect Movement began
  • 1937–1940 — First Anti-Hindi agitation
  • 1938 — Periyar assumed Justice Party leadership
  • 27 August 1944 — Justice Party transformed into Dravidar Kazhagam
  • 1945 — Black Shirt Volunteer organisation developed
  • May 1946 — Black Shirt conference at Madurai
  • 17 September 1949 — DMK founded
  • 1952 — Parasakthi released
  • 15 July 1953 — Kallakudi agitation
  • 1953–1954 — Opposition to modified elementary-education scheme
  • 1957 — DMK won 15 Assembly seats
  • 1961 — E. V. K. Sampath left DMK
  • 1962 — DMK won 50 Assembly seats
  • 1963 — DMK abandoned separate Dravida Nadu demand
  • January–February 1965 — Major Anti-Hindi agitation
  • 1967 — DMK won the state election
  • 1967 — Anna became Chief Minister
  • 1967 — Self-Respect marriages legally recognised through the Tamil Nadu amendment
  • 1967 — Two-language policy associated with Anna’s government
  • 1968 — Madras State alteration-of-name law enacted
  • 14 January 1969 — Name Tamil Nadu came into effect
  • February 1969 — Death of Anna
  • 1972 — MGR founded ADMK
  • 1977 — MGR became Chief Minister
  • Later period — ADMK became AIADMK
Organisation–Leader Associations
  • Justice Party — Theagaraya Chetty, T. M. Nair and Natesa Mudaliar
  • Self-Respect Movement — Periyar
  • Dravidar Kazhagam — Periyar
  • DMK — C. N. Annadurai
  • AIADMK — M. G. Ramachandran
Organisation–Year Associations
  • Justice Party — 1916
  • Self-Respect Movement — 1925
  • Dravidar Kazhagam — 1944
  • DMK — 1949
  • ADMK — 1972
Publication–Leader Associations
  • Kudi Arasu — Periyar
  • Viduthalai — Justice Party and later DK
  • Dravida Nadu — Anna
  • Murasoli — Karunanidhi
  • Nam Naadu — DMK
Leader–Medium Associations
  • Periyar — Propaganda tours, newspapers and social campaigns
  • Anna — Oratory, theatre and journalism
  • Karunanidhi — Journalism, drama and film dialogue
  • MGR — Cinema, fan associations and electoral mobilisation
  • Bharathidasan — Poetry and Dravidian social ideas
  • Sathyavani Muthu — Adi Dravida representation within DMK politics
High-Yield Distinctions
Linguistic Dravidian versus Political Dravidian

Linguistic Dravidian

  • Language-family classification
  • Tamil, Telugu, Kannada, Malayalam and other languages

Political Dravidian

  • Identity used in social and political movements
  • Anti-caste, regional and cultural meanings
Non-Brahmin Movement versus Dravidian Movement

Non-Brahmin Movement

  • Focused initially on representation
  • Education and employment
  • Broad coalition outside Brahmin groups

Dravidian Movement

  • Included cultural identity
  • Rationalism
  • Language
  • Social reform
  • State power

The Dravidian Movement grew from, but became broader than, early non-Brahmin politics.

Justice Party versus Self-Respect Movement

Justice Party

  • Electoral party
  • Formed governments
  • Communal representation

Self-Respect Movement

  • Social movement
  • Marriage, caste, women and rationalism
Justice Party versus Dravidar Kazhagam

Justice Party

  • Founded in 1916
  • Contested elections
  • Provincial ministries

Dravidar Kazhagam

  • Created in 1944
  • Non-electoral
  • Social and ideological movement
Dravidar Kazhagam versus DMK

DK

  • Periyar
  • Non-electoral
  • Social transformation

DMK

  • Anna
  • Founded in 1949
  • Electoral political party
Periyar versus Anna

Periyar

  • Preferred non-electoral social revolution
  • Led DK

Anna

  • Supported democratic electoral participation
  • Founded DMK

They shared several social objectives but differed over political method.

DK Flag versus DMK Flag

DK

  • Black field
  • Red circle

DMK

  • Red and black horizontal colours
  • Rising Sun electoral symbol
Dravida Nadu versus State Autonomy

Dravida Nadu

  • Separate political unit
  • Early demand

State autonomy

  • Greater state powers within India
  • Later DMK position
First versus Second Anti-Hindi Agitation

1937–1940

  • Compulsory Hindi in provincial schools
  • Rajaji ministry

1965

  • Union official-language issue
  • Strong student participation
  • Major factor in Congress defeat
1957 versus 1962 Election

1957

  • First major DMK electoral participation
  • 15 seats

1962

  • 50 seats
  • Principal opposition
Kallakudi versus Anti-Hindi Agitation

Kallakudi

  • Place-name and regional dignity
  • 1953
  • Karunanidhi

Anti-Hindi

  • Language policy
  • Statewide mobilisation
  • Major phases in 1937 and 1965
DMK versus AIADMK

DMK

  • Founded by Anna in 1949
  • First formed government in 1967

AIADMK

  • Founded by MGR as ADMK in 1972
  • First formed government in 1977
Social Movement versus Political Party

Social movement

  • Changes ideas and social practices
  • Example — DK

Political party

  • Contests elections and forms governments
  • Examples — DMK and AIADMK
Exam Traps
  • Dravidian originally referred to a language family before acquiring political meaning.
  • Ellis’s linguistic argument preceded Caldwell’s work.
  • Justice Party was founded in 1916.
  • Self-Respect Movement began in 1925.
  • Periyar was not a founder of the original Justice Party.
  • Justice Party became Dravidar Kazhagam in 1944.
  • DK did not ordinarily contest elections.
  • DMK was founded on 17 September 1949.
  • The DMK founding meeting was held at Robinson Park, Royapuram.
  • Anna was the principal founder of DMK.
  • The DMK split cannot be explained solely by Periyar’s marriage to Maniammai.
  • Parasakthi was released in 1952.
  • Kallakudi agitation occurred on 15 July 1953.
  • The modified education scheme was criticised as Kula Kalvi Thittam.
  • DMK won 15 seats in 1957.
  • DMK won 50 seats in 1962.
  • DMK abandoned the separate Dravida Nadu demand in 1963.
  • The 1965 agitation concerned the Union official-language issue.
  • Not every incident in 1965 was directly organised by the DMK.
  • DMK formed the government in 1967.
  • Anna became Chief Minister in 1967.
  • The name Tamil Nadu legally came into effect on 14 January 1969.
  • MGR founded ADMK in 1972.
  • ADMK later became AIADMK.
  • DK, DMK and AIADMK are related but distinct organisations.
  • Detailed Dravidian principles belong to Chapter 27.
  • Periyar’s complete contribution belongs to Chapter 28.
  • Anna’s complete contribution belongs to Chapter 29.
